answer:
**Biot-Savart law.** The magnetic induction produced at a point by a small current element is directly proportional to the current, to the length of the element, and to the sine of the angle between the element and the line joining it to the point, and is inversely proportional to the square of the distance of the point from the element.

Consider a conductor carrying a current \(I\). Let \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l}\) be a small current-length element of it, and let \(P\) be a point at a distance \(r\) from this element, the position vector of \(P\) with respect to the element making an angle \(\theta\) with \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l}\).

The magnitude \(\mathrm{d}B\) of the magnetic induction at \(P\) due to this element satisfies

\(\mathrm{d}B \propto I\), \(\quad \mathrm{d}B \propto \mathrm{d}l\), \(\quad \mathrm{d}B \propto \sin\theta\), \(\quad \mathrm{d}B \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\)

Combining the four,

\(\mathrm{d}B \propto \dfrac{I\,\mathrm{d}l\,\sin\theta}{r^{2}}\)

\(\therefore \mathrm{d}B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,\mathrm{d}l\,\sin\theta}{r^{2}}\)

where \(\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\) is the constant of proportionality for free space, \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) T m/A being the permeability of free space.

**Vector form.**

\(\mathrm{d}\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,\mathrm{d}\vec{l} \times \hat{r}}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,\mathrm{d}\vec{l} \times \vec{r}}{r^{3}}\)

**Direction.** \(\mathrm{d}\vec{B}\) is perpendicular to the plane containing \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l}\) and \(\vec{r}\), its sense being given by the right-handed screw rule applied to \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l} \times \hat{r}\).

**Total field.** The whole conductor is the sum of such elements, so

\(\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi}\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{l} \times \hat{r}}{r^{2}}\)

Two limiting cases follow at once from this expression. \(\mathrm{d}B = 0\) when \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\) or \(\theta = 180^{\circ}\), so a straight segment produces no field at points lying on its own line; and \(\mathrm{d}B\) is greatest when \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\), which is the case for every element of a circular arc taken about its own centre.

**Formula for a circular arc.** For a wire bent into a circular arc of radius \(R\) carrying a current \(I\), the magnetic induction at the centre of the arc, when the arc subtends an angle \(\theta\) (in radian) at that centre, is

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi R}\,\theta\)

**Deriving it from the Biot-Savart law.** Every current-length element \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l}\) of the arc is perpendicular to the radius vector \(\vec{R}\) drawn from it to the centre, so \(\sin 90^{\circ} = 1\) and

\(\mathrm{d}B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,\mathrm{d}l\,\sin 90^{\circ}}{R^{2}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,\mathrm{d}l}{R^{2}}\)

Every element gives \(\mathrm{d}\vec{B}\) along the same normal to the plane of the arc, so the magnitudes simply add. The length of the arc is \(l = R\theta\), hence

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{I}{R^{2}}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{R\theta}\mathrm{d}l = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{I}{R^{2}}(R\theta)\)

\(\therefore B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I\theta}{4\pi R}\)

**Magnetic induction at the centre of a complete circular loop.** A full loop is the arc for which \(\theta = 2\pi\) radian:

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi R}\times 2\pi\)

\(\therefore B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{2R}\)

For a closely wound coil of \(N\) such turns each turn contributes equally, giving \(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}NI}{2R}\).

The result is consistent with the half-turn case: a semicircular arc has \(\theta = \pi\) and gives \(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{4R}\), exactly half the full-loop value, as it must. The field is directed along the axis of the loop, its sense given by the right-hand rule applied to the circulating current.

Given: \(I = 6\) A, \(d = 3\) cm \(= 0.03\) m, \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) T m/A.

For a very long straight wire the magnetic induction at a perpendicular distance \(d\) is

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 6}{2\pi \times 0.03} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 6}{0.03} = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{-6}}{0.03}\)

\(\therefore B = 4 \times 10^{-5}\) T

Check by substituting back: \(I = \dfrac{2\pi d B}{\mu_{0}} = \dfrac{0.03 \times 4 \times 10^{-5}}{2 \times 10^{-7}} = 6\) A, the current given.

The field lines are concentric circles round the wire lying in the plane perpendicular to it, the sense being given by the right-hand grip rule.

Given: \(N = 200\) turns, \(R = 10\) cm \(= 0.10\) m, \(I = 0.5\) A, \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) T m/A.

The turns are closely wound, so each of the \(N\) turns contributes equally at the centre and

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}NI}{2R} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 200 \times 0.5}{2 \times 0.10} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 100}{0.20}\)

\(\therefore B = 2\pi \times 10^{-4} = 6.283 \times 10^{-4}\) T

Check: one turn alone would give \(\dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{2R} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times 0.5}{0.20} = 3.142\times10^{-6}\) T, and \(200\) times this is \(6.283\times10^{-4}\) T, the same value.

The field is directed along the axis of the coil, in the sense given by the right-hand rule.

**Ampere's circuital law.** The line integral of the magnetic induction \(\vec{B}\) taken round any closed path in free space is equal to \(\mu_{0}\) times the net current crossing the area bounded by that path:

\(\displaystyle\oint \vec{B}\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec{l} = \mu_{0}I_{\text{enclosed}}\)

**Explanation.** The closed path is called an Amperian loop and may be of any shape. \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l}\) is a small length element of the loop, taken in the sense in which the loop is traversed, and \(\vec{B}\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec{l} = B\,\mathrm{d}l\cos\alpha\), where \(\alpha\) is the angle between \(\vec{B}\) and \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l}\). A current is counted positive if it is related to the sense of traversal by the right-handed screw rule, and negative if it is oppositely directed; only the currents that actually pass through the area bounded by the loop enter \(I_{\text{enclosed}}\). Currents lying outside the loop do contribute to \(\vec{B}\) at points of the loop, but their contributions to the integral cancel and add nothing to it.

The law is useful because, where the configuration is symmetrical enough that \(\vec{B}\) is of constant magnitude and everywhere tangential to a suitably chosen loop, \(\vec{B}\) can be taken out of the integral and found without integrating the Biot-Savart law.

**Illustration - a long straight wire.** Take as the Amperian loop a circle of radius \(r\) centred on the wire and lying in the plane perpendicular to it. By symmetry \(\vec{B}\) has the same magnitude at every point of this circle and is tangential to it, so \(\alpha = 0^{\circ}\):

\(\displaystyle\oint \vec{B}\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec{l} = B\displaystyle\oint \mathrm{d}l = B(2\pi r) = \mu_{0}I\)

\(\therefore B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}\)

This is the same expression as the Biot-Savart law gives for a long straight wire, which is the check on the law.

A toroid is a solenoid bent round on itself into a closed ring, the \(N\) turns being wound uniformly over the ring. The axis of a toroid is the circular centre-line of its winding, and it is along this circle, of mean radius \(r\), that the magnetic induction inside the toroid is directed; the expression below is obtained for points on it.

**Choice of Amperian loop.** Take the circle of radius \(r\) that is itself the axis of the toroid. By the symmetry of the winding, \(\vec{B}\) has the same magnitude at every point of this circle and is directed tangentially to it, i.e. along \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l}\) at every point.

**Applying Ampere's circuital law.**

\(\displaystyle\oint \vec{B}\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec{l} = \mu_{0}I_{\text{enclosed}}\)

Since \(\vec{B}\) is parallel to \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l}\) and constant in magnitude,

\(\displaystyle\oint \vec{B}\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec{l} = B\displaystyle\oint \mathrm{d}l = B(2\pi r)\)

Each of the \(N\) turns of the winding crosses the area bounded by this loop once, and each carries the current \(I\), so \(I_{\text{enclosed}} = NI\). Hence

\(B(2\pi r) = \mu_{0}NI\)

\(\therefore B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}NI}{2\pi r}\)

Writing \(n = \dfrac{N}{2\pi r}\) for the number of turns per unit length of the toroid, this is

\(\therefore B = \mu_{0}nI\)

which is the same expression as for a long solenoid, and that is the check on the result: bending a long solenoid into a ring does not alter the field inside it.

Outside the toroid the field is zero. An Amperian circle drawn in the plane of the ring but of radius smaller than the inner radius encloses no turn at all, and one of radius larger than the outer radius is crossed by each turn twice, once going in and once coming out, so in both cases \(I_{\text{enclosed}} = 0\) and hence \(B = 0\).
twin: A toroid of narrow radius of 10 cm has 1000 turns of wire. For a magnetic field of \(5 \times 10^{-2}\) T along its axis, how much current is required to be passed through the wire?

answer:
Given: length \(L = \pi\) m, diameter \(= 5\) cm, \(N = 1000\) turns, \(I = 5\) A.

Number of turns per unit length:

\(n = \dfrac{N}{L} = \dfrac{1000}{\pi}\) turns/m

For a long solenoid the magnetic induction at the centre, on the axis, is

\(B = \mu_{0}nI = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{1000}{\pi} \times 5 = 4 \times 10^{-7} \times 1000 \times 5\)

\(\therefore B = 2 \times 10^{-3}\) T

The \(\pi\) of \(\mu_{0}\) cancels against the \(\pi\) in the length, which is why the answer comes out exact.

Check by substituting back: \(n = \dfrac{B}{\mu_{0}I} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-3}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 5} = 318.3\) turns/m, and \(\dfrac{1000}{\pi} = 318.3\) turns/m, the same value.

The diameter does not enter the expression: for a long solenoid the axial field depends only on \(n\) and \(I\), and the 5 cm diameter serves only to confirm that the solenoid is long compared with its width. The field is directed along the axis.

The labelled diagram of a cyclotron shows the following parts.

- **Dees \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\)** - two hollow, semicircular, D-shaped metal chambers of copper or brass, mounted with their diameters facing each other and separated by a narrow gap. They are the electrodes inside which the charged particle travels.
- **High-frequency alternating voltage source** - connected across the two dees, marked as an oscillator of frequency \(f\). It maintains an alternating electric field in the gap between the dees.
- **Electromagnet with pole pieces N and S** - a large magnet whose flat circular poles are placed one above and one below the dees, producing a strong uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) directed perpendicular to the plane of the dees.
- **Ion source S** - placed at the centre of the gap between the dees, where the charged particles to be accelerated are produced.
- **Evacuated chamber** - the whole assembly of dees is enclosed in a vacuum chamber, so that the particles are not scattered by collisions with air molecules.
- **Deflecting plate and exit window (target)** - at the rim of one dee, to lead the fast particles out of the machine on to the target.
- The **spiral path** of the accelerated particle is shown starting at the ion source and widening turn by turn until it reaches the rim of the dee, where its radius equals the radius of the dee.

Inside a dee the particle is shielded from the electric field and only the magnetic field acts on it, bending it into a semicircle; in the gap only the electric field acts, and it accelerates the particle. Each crossing of the gap increases the speed, so the radius \(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}\) of the next semicircle is larger, and the path is a spiral of increasing radius.

Given: \(B = 1.4\) Wb/m\(^{2}\), protons of mass \(M_{p} = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg and charge \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C, \(\pi = 3.142\).

Inside a dee the magnetic force provides the centripetal force, \(evB = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}\), so \(r = \dfrac{mv}{eB}\) and the time for one full revolution is

\(T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{eB}\)

which is independent of the speed and of the radius. Substituting,

\(T = \dfrac{2 \times 3.142 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.4} = \dfrac{1.049 \times 10^{-26}}{2.24 \times 10^{-19}}\)

\(\therefore T = 4.685 \times 10^{-8}\) s

The proton crosses the gap between the two dees twice in each revolution, and it must be accelerated at every crossing. The electric field between the dees must therefore be reversed once every half period:

\(t = \dfrac{T}{2} = \dfrac{4.685 \times 10^{-8}}{2}\)

\(\therefore t = 2.342 \times 10^{-8}\) s

The electric field must be reversed once every \(2.342 \times 10^{-8}\) s.

Check: the corresponding oscillator frequency is \(\dfrac{1}{T} = 2.134 \times 10^{7}\) Hz, which is the cyclotron frequency \(\dfrac{eB}{2\pi m} = \dfrac{2.24 \times 10^{-19}}{1.049 \times 10^{-26}} = 2.135 \times 10^{7}\) Hz, the same value.
twin: For proton acceleration, a cyclotron is used in which a magnetic field of 1.4 Wb/m\(^2\) is applied. Find the time period for reversing the electric field between the two Ds.

answer:
Given: kinetic energy of the protons \(= 5\) MeV, \(B = 2\) T, speed of the proton \(v = 3 \times 10^{7}\) m/s. Take \(m_{p} = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg and \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C.

**Radius.** At the rim of the dee the magnetic force supplies the centripetal force:

\(evB = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}\)

\(\therefore r = \dfrac{mv}{eB} = \dfrac{1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times 3 \times 10^{7}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2} = \dfrac{5.01 \times 10^{-20}}{3.2 \times 10^{-19}}\)

\(\therefore r = 0.1566\) m \(= 15.66\) cm

**Frequency of the applied alternating voltage.** The oscillator must keep step with the revolution of the proton, so its frequency is the cyclotron frequency

\(f = \dfrac{v}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{eB}{2\pi m} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2}{2\pi \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}} = \dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{-19}}{1.049 \times 10^{-26}}\)

\(\therefore f = 3.05 \times 10^{7}\) Hz \(= 30.5\) MHz

Check on the data: the kinetic energy carried by the quoted speed is \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times (3 \times 10^{7})^{2} = 7.515 \times 10^{-13}\) J \(= 4.70\) MeV, which agrees with the stated 5 MeV to the accuracy of the rounded speed - the exact 5 MeV would correspond to \(v = 3.10 \times 10^{7}\) m/s and \(r = 16.15\) cm. The frequency is unaffected either way, since it does not depend on the speed.

The net force on a closed circuit placed in a uniform magnetic field is **zero**.

The force on a current-length element \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l}\) of a circuit carrying a current \(I\) in a field \(\vec{B}\) is \(\mathrm{d}\vec{F} = I\,\mathrm{d}\vec{l} \times \vec{B}\). Summing round the whole circuit,

\(\vec{F} = \displaystyle\oint I\,\mathrm{d}\vec{l} \times \vec{B}\)

For a uniform field \(\vec{B}\), both \(I\) and \(\vec{B}\) are the same at every element and may be taken outside the integral:

\(\vec{F} = I\left(\displaystyle\oint \mathrm{d}\vec{l}\right) \times \vec{B}\)

The vector sum of the length elements taken right round a closed path is zero, because the path returns to its starting point:

\(\displaystyle\oint \mathrm{d}\vec{l} = 0\)

\(\therefore \vec{F} = 0\)

The circuit may still experience a torque, which is what turns the coil of a moving coil galvanometer; it is only the resultant force that vanishes.

answer:
The work done is **zero**.

The magnetic force on a charge \(q\) moving with velocity \(\vec{v}\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) is

\(\vec{F} = q\,\vec{v} \times \vec{B}\)

By the definition of the vector product, \(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\), so \(\vec{F}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\) at every instant. In a small time \(\mathrm{d}t\) the charge is displaced by \(\mathrm{d}\vec{r} = \vec{v}\,\mathrm{d}t\), and the work done in that displacement is

\(\mathrm{d}W = \vec{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec{r} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\cdot\vec{v}\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\)

since \((\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\cdot\vec{v} = 0\).

\(\therefore W = \displaystyle\int \mathrm{d}W = 0\)

A magnetic field therefore never does work on a moving charge. Consistently with this, the kinetic energy \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\) and hence the speed of the charge remain unchanged; the field alters only the direction of \(\vec{v}\), bending the charge here into a circular path, since \(\vec{v}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\).

Given: separation \(d = 1.35\) cm \(= 1.35 \times 10^{-2}\) m, force per unit length \(\dfrac{F}{L} = 4.76 \times 10^{-2}\) N/m, and equal currents, so \(I_{1} = I_{2} = I\).

The force per unit length between two long parallel current-carrying wires is

\(\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I^{2}}{2\pi d}\)

\(\therefore I^{2} = \dfrac{(F/L)\,2\pi d}{\mu_{0}} = \dfrac{4.76 \times 10^{-2} \times 1.35 \times 10^{-2}}{2 \times 10^{-7}} = \dfrac{6.426 \times 10^{-4}}{2 \times 10^{-7}} = 3213\)

\(\therefore I = \sqrt{3213} = 56.68\) A

Check by substituting back: \(\dfrac{\mu_{0}I^{2}}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 3213}{1.35 \times 10^{-2}} = 4.76 \times 10^{-2}\) N/m, the force per unit length given.

The force is attractive if the two currents are in the same direction and repulsive if they are oppositely directed.

For a current-carrying coil of \(N\) turns, each of area \(A\), carrying a current \(I\), the magnetic dipole moment is

\(\vec{m} = NI\vec{A}\)

where \(\vec{A}\) is the area vector, directed along the normal to the plane of the coil in the sense given by the right-hand rule applied to the circulating current.

The torque acting on the coil when it is placed in a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) is, in vector form,

\(\vec{\tau} = \vec{m} \times \vec{B}\)

and in terms of the coil's own quantities, \(\vec{\tau} = NI\vec{A} \times \vec{B}\).

Its magnitude is \(\tau = mB\sin\theta = NIAB\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec{m}\) and \(\vec{B}\). The torque is therefore greatest when the plane of the coil contains \(\vec{B}\) (\(\theta = 90^{\circ}\)) and zero when \(\vec{m}\) is parallel to \(\vec{B}\), which is the position of stable equilibrium.

Given: \(N = 300\) turns, diameter \(= 14\) cm so radius \(R = 7\) cm \(= 0.07\) m, \(I = 15\) A.

Area enclosed by one turn:

\(A = \pi R^{2} = \pi \times (0.07)^{2} = \pi \times 4.9 \times 10^{-3} = 1.539 \times 10^{-2}\) m\(^{2}\)

The magnetic dipole moment of a coil of \(N\) turns is

\(m = NIA = 300 \times 15 \times 1.539 \times 10^{-2} = 4500 \times 1.539 \times 10^{-2}\)

\(\therefore m = 69.27\) A m\(^{2}\)

Check by a second route, using the diameter directly: \(m = NI\dfrac{\pi D^{2}}{4} = 300 \times 15 \times \dfrac{\pi \times (0.14)^{2}}{4} = 4500 \times 1.539 \times 10^{-2} = 69.27\) A m\(^{2}\), the same value.

The magnetic dipole moment is directed along the axis of the coil, in the sense given by the right-hand rule.

The labelled diagram of a suspended coil type moving coil galvanometer shows the following parts.

- **Coil** - a rectangular coil of a large number of turns of fine, insulated copper wire, wound on a light non-metallic frame (or on a metallic frame where damping is wanted), suspended between the poles of the magnet.
- **Permanent horseshoe magnet with concave pole pieces N and S** - it provides a strong magnetic field in the region of the coil. The pole pieces are cylindrically concave.
- **Soft iron cylinder** - a cylindrical piece of soft iron fixed coaxially inside the coil, without touching it. Together with the concave pole pieces it makes the field **radial**, so that the plane of the coil is parallel to \(\vec{B}\) in every position of the coil, and it also concentrates the field lines by drawing them into itself.
- **Phosphor bronze suspension fibre** - a thin fibre from which the coil hangs, its upper end attached to a **torsion head**. It leads the current into the coil and provides the restoring couple, and the torsion head is used to set the coil at the zero of the scale.
- **Lower spring (hair spring) with terminal** - a loosely wound spring or fine wire at the bottom of the coil, through which the current leaves the coil, offering almost no opposition to the rotation.
- **Small plane mirror** - fixed to the suspension fibre above the coil; with a **lamp and scale arrangement**, the spot of light reflected from it measures the deflection of the coil.
- **Terminals \(T_{1}\) and \(T_{2}\)** on the case, and a **levelling base with levelling screws**.

Because the field is radial, the deflecting torque is \(NIAB\) in every position of the coil, and it is balanced by the restoring torque \(k\theta\) of the suspension fibre, so \(NIAB = k\theta\) and the deflection \(\theta\) is directly proportional to the current \(I\), giving the instrument a uniform (linear) scale.

**Advantages of a moving coil galvanometer.**

- It is very sensitive: currents of the order of \(10^{-12}\) A can be detected, because the restoring couple of the fine suspension fibre is very small.
- Its scale is uniform (linear), since the radial field makes the deflection directly proportional to the current, so the instrument can be calibrated directly.
- It is not affected by stray magnetic fields, the field of its own permanent magnet being strong compared with them.
- The deflection is steady, and by winding the coil on a metallic frame the eddy currents induced in the frame make the instrument dead-beat.

**Disadvantages of a moving coil galvanometer.**

- It can be used only for direct current; with alternating current the deflection reverses each half cycle and the coil merely vibrates about the zero.
- The suspension fibre is delicate, so the instrument is fragile, must be levelled and handled carefully, and is not portable.
- Its sensitivity cannot be changed at will, being fixed by \(N\), \(A\), \(B\) and \(k\).
- It needs a lamp and scale arrangement to read small deflections, and a large current may burn out the fine coil.

**Numerical.** Given: \(N = 10\) turns, length \(l = 12\) cm \(= 0.12\) m, breadth \(b = 8\) cm \(= 0.08\) m, \(I = 125\ \mu\text{A} = 125 \times 10^{-6}\) A, \(B = 10^{-2}\) T with the coil perpendicular to the field, twist constant \(k = 12 \times 10^{-9}\) Nm/degree.

Area of the coil:

\(A = l \times b = 0.12 \times 0.08 = 9.6 \times 10^{-3}\) m\(^{2}\)

At equilibrium the deflecting torque on the coil is balanced by the restoring torque of the suspension fibre:

\(NIAB = k\theta\)

\(\therefore \theta = \dfrac{NIAB}{k} = \dfrac{10 \times 125 \times 10^{-6} \times 9.6 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{-2}}{12 \times 10^{-9}} = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{-7}}{1.2 \times 10^{-8}}\)

\(\therefore \theta = 10^{\circ}\)

Check: at this deflection the restoring torque is \(k\theta = 12 \times 10^{-9} \times 10 = 1.2 \times 10^{-7}\) N m, equal to the deflecting torque \(NIAB = 1.2 \times 10^{-7}\) N m computed above, so the two balance.

Since \(k\) is quoted per degree, \(\theta\) comes out in degrees and no conversion to radian is needed.

Given: \(N = 100\) turns, \(A = 15\) cm\(^{2} = 15 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^{2}\), radial field \(B = 0.03\) T, twist constant of the suspension fibre \(k = 15 \times 10^{-10}\) N-m/degree.

In the radial field of a moving coil galvanometer the plane of the coil is always parallel to \(\vec{B}\), so the deflecting torque is \(NIAB\) in every position. At equilibrium it is balanced by the restoring torque \(k\theta\) of the suspension fibre:

\(NIAB = k\theta\)

The current sensitivity is the deflection produced per unit current:

\(S_{i} = \dfrac{\theta}{I} = \dfrac{NAB}{k}\)

\(S_{i} = \dfrac{100 \times 15 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.03}{15 \times 10^{-10}} = \dfrac{4.5 \times 10^{-3}}{1.5 \times 10^{-9}}\)

\(\therefore S_{i} = 3 \times 10^{6}\) degree/ampere

Check: a current of \(1\ \mu\text{A}\) would give \(\theta = 3 \times 10^{6} \times 10^{-6} = 3^{\circ}\), a deflection that is readable, which is consistent with the instrument being a sensitive galvanometer.

The sensitivity may therefore also be quoted as \(3\) degree per microampere.
twin: A moving coil galvanometer has been fitted with a rectangular coil having 50 turns and dimensions 5 cm \(\times\) 3 cm. The radial magnetic field in which the coil is suspended is of 0.05 Wb/m\(^2\). The torsional constant of the spring is \(1.5 \times 10^{-9}\) Nm/degree. Obtain the current required to be passed through the galvanometer so as to produce a deflection of \(30^\circ\).

answer:
**(D)** tesla

The weber (Wb) is the SI unit of magnetic flux \(\Phi\). Magnetic flux through an area \(A\) held perpendicular to a uniform magnetic induction \(B\) is

\(\Phi = BA\)

\(\therefore B = \dfrac{\Phi}{A}\)

So \(\text{Wb m}^{-2}\) is the unit of magnetic flux per unit area, that is, of the magnetic induction (magnetic flux density) \(B\). The SI unit of magnetic induction is the tesla, defined by \(1\ \text{T} = 1\ \text{Wb m}^{-2}\).

The other units named belong to other quantities: the henry is the SI unit of inductance (\(1\ \text{H} = 1\ \text{Wb A}^{-1}\)), the watt is the SI unit of power (\(1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J s}^{-1}\)) and the dyne is the CGS unit of force (\(1\ \text{dyne} = 10^{-5}\) N).
